items.prompt: State the four things that are bonded to the central carbon atom of an amino acid.
items.canonical_answer: An amino group (–NH2), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen atom and an R group.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: all four features named. The R group is the part that differs between amino acids; naming a phosphate or a hydroxyl group in its place does not earn the mark, because the hydroxyl is already part of the carboxyl group.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: Describe how a peptide bond forms between two amino acids.
items.canonical_answer: The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the other react in a condensation reaction. An –OH from the carboxyl group and an H from the amino group are removed together as a molecule of water, and a C–N peptide bond forms between the carbon and the nitrogen.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the groups that react, the carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the other, with water removed (1); the C–N peptide bond forms as a result (1).
An answer in which water is added, or in which the R groups join, describes the reverse reaction or the wrong atoms and earns neither mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: A learner writes that two amino acids are joined by a "dipeptide bond". Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion between the product and the bond. The bond is a peptide bond. In fact a dipeptide is the molecule made of two amino acids joined by that bond, which forms by condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the other. The test is to ask what the bond is called and which groups form it: it is a peptide bond, formed by a carboxyl group and an amino group.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error identified, that dipeptide names the molecule and not the bond (1); the correct idea, a peptide bond formed by condensation between a carboxyl group and an amino group (1).
The card is a discrimination between the molecule and its bond, not a repeat of how a dipeptide forms.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt:
A table gives the relative molecular mass of three amino acids and of the tripeptide made from them.

| Substance | Relative molecular mass |
|---|---|
| glycine | 75 |
| alanine | 89 |
| serine | 105 |
| tripeptide of glycine, alanine and serine | 233 |

Describe what the values show about how the tripeptide formed.
items.canonical_answer: The three amino acids together have a relative molecular mass of 75 + 89 + 105 = 269, but the tripeptide is 233, which is 269 - 233 = 36 lower. One molecule of water has a relative molecular mass of 18, and 2 × 18 = 36. The values show that two molecules of water were lost, one for each of the two peptide bonds formed in condensation reactions.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the table values compared, the total of the amino acids is 36 higher than the tripeptide (1); the difference means two molecules of water were lost, one for each peptide bond, so the amino acids joined by condensation (1).
A reading of the figures that does not link 36 to water earns one mark at most.

items.prompt: State what is meant by the primary structure of a protein.
items.canonical_answer: The primary structure of a protein is the sequence of amino acids in its polypeptide chain.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, sequence (or order) of amino acids in the polypeptide. A statement about coiling or folding describes secondary or tertiary structure, not the primary structure.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: Explain how the primary structure of a polypeptide determines its tertiary structure.
items.canonical_answer: The sequence of amino acids sets which R groups lie at which positions along the chain. The R groups then interact with each other, through hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions, at particular places, which folds the chain into one specific three-dimensional shape. A different sequence would bring different R groups together, so it would fold into a different shape.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the sequence fixes the positions of the R groups (1); the R groups interact at particular places, which folds the chain into one specific shape, so a different sequence gives a different shape (1).
Naming the sequence without saying how the R groups cause the folding earns one mark at most.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: A learner explains that the alpha helix of secondary structure is held in place by hydrogen bonds between R groups. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is to bring R groups into secondary structure. In fact the hydrogen bonds of an alpha helix form along the backbone, between the C=O of one peptide link and the N–H of another. Interactions between R groups belong to tertiary structure, not secondary. The test is to ask whether the R groups or the backbone form the hydrogen bonds: in an alpha helix it is the backbone.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error identified, R groups wrongly named as forming the hydrogen bonds of secondary structure (1); the correct idea, hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N–H of the backbone, with R group interactions belonging to tertiary structure (1).
The card discriminates two levels of structure; a description of the alpha helix alone does not earn the second mark unless the backbone is named.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt:
A laboratory reports the polypeptide chains in two proteins.

| Protein | Number of polypeptide chains | Amino acids in each chain |
|---|---|---|
| P | 1 | 150 |
| Q | 4 | 210, 210, 330, 330 |

Describe what the table shows about the quaternary structure of the two proteins.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that protein Q has a quaternary structure, because it is made of four polypeptide chains assembled into one protein. Protein P has a single chain, so it has no quaternary structure and its highest level is the tertiary structure. Protein Q has 210 + 210 + 330 + 330 = 1080 amino acids in all, in four chains, while protein P has 150 in one.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: Q has a quaternary structure because it has more than one polypeptide chain (1); P has a single chain, so no quaternary structure, and its highest level is tertiary (1).
The values for amino acids per chain do not decide the matter: the number of chains is the reading that means quaternary structure. A total of 1080 is a creditworthy extra point; the tariff is 2.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a disulfide bond in a protein.
items.canonical_answer: A disulfide bond is a covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of the R groups of two cysteine residues.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteines. A statement that it forms between hydrogen and oxygen describes a hydrogen bond.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: State where the non-polar R groups are found in a folded protein that works in water.
items.canonical_answer: In the interior of the protein, clustered together and away from the water.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature of the structure, the non-polar R groups lie in the interior, away from the water. The polar and charged R groups lie on the outside, so an answer that places non-polar R groups on the outer surface is incorrect.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: A learner says that hydrogen bonds and disulfide bonds are the same kind of bond and hold a protein together equally strongly. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of two different bonds. A disulfide bond is a covalent bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteines, and it is strong. A hydrogen bond is an attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen and a slightly negative atom, and each one is weak, although a protein has very many of them. The test is to ask which one is covalent, and between which atoms: the disulfide bond, between sulfur atoms.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that the two bonds are treated as the same and equally strong (1); the correct contrast, the disulfide bond is covalent between sulfur atoms of cysteines and strong, whereas a hydrogen bond is weak individually (1).
The card is a discrimination, not a repeat of either definition.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt:
Two proteins were treated in the laboratory with a chemical that breaks disulfide bonds and no other bonds. These are our readings.

| Protein | Disulfide bonds before treatment | Shape after treatment |
|---|---|---|
| A | 4 | large loss of shape |
| B | 0 | no change |

Describe what the data show about the bonds that hold protein A and protein B in shape.
items.canonical_answer: The data show that the shape of protein A depends on its four disulfide bonds, because it lost shape when they were broken. Protein B has no disulfide bonds and did not change, so its shape is held by other interactions, such as hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and hydrophobic interactions.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: protein A lost shape when its disulfide bonds were broken, so they hold its shape (1); protein B has no disulfide bonds and did not change, so other interactions hold it (1).
The table gives data for these two proteins only, so a general claim about all proteins is not supported by it.

items.prompt: State the number of polypeptide chains in one haemoglobin molecule and name them.
items.canonical_answer: Four: two alpha-globin chains and two beta-globin chains.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the structure given in full, four chains, two alpha (α-globin) and two beta (β-globin). A statement of four without the names, or of the number of red blood cells, does not earn the mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: Describe how the structure of a collagen molecule and of a collagen fibre makes collagen strong.
items.canonical_answer: A collagen molecule is three polypeptide chains wound together in a triple helix. In a fibre, many molecules lie side by side, staggered, and are joined by cross-links between neighbouring molecules. The cross-links stop the molecules sliding past one another, so the fibre resists being pulled.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: a molecule is a triple helix of three polypeptide chains (1); a fibre is many molecules joined by cross-links, which stop them sliding, so it resists pulling (1).
The molecule and the fibre must be kept apart: a statement that a fibre is a triple helix mixes the two.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: A butcher in Oshakati cuts a tendon from a cow. The tendon is tough and does not dissolve in water, whereas the haemoglobin in the cow's blood is dissolved in the red blood cells. Using the information given, explain how the structure of collagen and the structure of haemoglobin suit these properties.
items.canonical_answer: The tendon is tough and insoluble because collagen is a fibrous protein: its triple-helix molecules are joined by cross-links into long fibres that resist pulling. Haemoglobin is dissolved because it is a globular protein with polar R groups on the outside of the molecule, which are attracted to water, so it is soluble.
marking_guidance: 2 marks, each tied to the case: collagen is a fibrous protein of cross-linked triple helices, so it is strong and insoluble (1); haemoglobin is globular with polar R groups on the outside, so it is soluble in the cytoplasm (1).
An answer that names globular and fibrous without tying each to the given property earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: A learner is asked to describe the structure of a haemoglobin molecule and writes about a red blood cell: it has no nucleus and is a biconcave disc. Explain the error, and state what the answer should include about the iron.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of the level: a cell is not a molecule. In fact a haemoglobin molecule has four polypeptide chains, each with one haem group, and each haem group holds one iron ion, Fe2+, which binds one oxygen molecule. The test is to ask how many haem groups one molecule has: four, so up to four oxygen molecules. "An ion" is not enough for the iron: the answer needs Fe2+ and the binding of oxygen.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, the cell described instead of the molecule (1); the correct molecule, four chains each with a haem group holding one Fe2+ that binds one oxygen molecule (1).
The test, how many haem groups one molecule has, separates the molecule from the cell. Naming the iron only as an ion earns no mark for the second point.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt:
A purified solution of haemoglobin was fully loaded with oxygen. These are our readings.

| Sample | Haemoglobin added (µmol) | Oxygen bound (µmol) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.25 | 1.00 |
| 2 | 0.50 | 2.00 |
| 3 | 0.75 | 3.00 |

Describe what the values show about how many oxygen molecules one haemoglobin molecule binds, and explain how this fits the structure of the molecule.
items.canonical_answer: In each sample the oxygen bound is four times the haemoglobin added: 1.00 ÷ 0.25 = 4 in sample 1. Likewise 2.00 ÷ 0.50 = 4 in sample 2, and 3.00 ÷ 0.75 = 4 in sample 3. This shows that one haemoglobin molecule binds four oxygen molecules, which fits the structure: it has four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group holding one Fe2+ that binds one oxygen molecule.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the values compared, the ratio of oxygen to haemoglobin is 4 to 1 in every sample, so four oxygen molecules per molecule (1); linked to four haem groups, each with one Fe2+ that binds one oxygen molecule (1).
The reading must use the table; a statement that haemoglobin carries oxygen, without the ratio, earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: State the importance of the iron in a haemoglobin molecule.
items.canonical_answer: Each haem group contains an Fe2+ ion, which binds one oxygen molecule reversibly, so haemoglobin can carry oxygen.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, the iron (Fe2+) binds oxygen. The statement that it gives the blood its red colour, or that it is an ion, is not the importance asked for.

items.prompt: Describe how to test a liquid food for protein with the biuret test, and the result that shows protein is present.
items.canonical_answer: First, put some of the liquid in a test tube. Then add an equal volume of sodium hydroxide solution, and add a few drops of dilute copper(II) sulfate solution and mix. No heating is needed. The result is a violet or purple colour if protein is present; if the mixture stays blue, protein is not detected.
marking_guidance: 3 marks in the correct order: the liquid and an equal volume of sodium hydroxide solution (1); a few drops of copper(II) sulfate solution (1); the result, violet or purple for protein and blue for none (1).
The sequence matters: copper(II) sulfate added without the alkali is not the biuret test. A step of heating, or the use of Benedict's solution or iodine, earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: State the reason that sodium hydroxide solution is added in the biuret test.
items.canonical_answer: The reaction between the copper(II) ions and the peptide bonds needs alkaline conditions.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason, the reaction needs alkaline conditions. A statement that the alkali dissolves the protein, or that it is added to speed up heating, is wrong.

items.prompt: A learner tests a solution of egg white for protein by adding Benedict's solution and warming it. The mixture stays blue, and the learner concludes that there is no protein. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is the use of the wrong test. Benedict's solution tests for reducing sugar, not protein, so a blue result says nothing about protein. In fact the biuret test is the test for protein: sodium hydroxide solution and then dilute copper(II) sulfate solution give a violet colour if peptide bonds are present. The test is to ask which test gives a violet colour with protein: the biuret test.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error, Benedict's tests for reducing sugar and a blue result does not show that protein is absent (1); the correct test, the biuret test, which gives violet with protein (1).
Iodine solution is the test for starch and is not accepted instead of the biuret test.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt:
A student carried out the biuret test in the same way on three extracts of equal volume. These are our observations.

| Extract | Colour after the test |
|---|---|
| boiled egg white | deep purple |
| sorghum porridge | pale lilac |
| sugar solution | blue |

Describe what the table shows about the protein in the extracts.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows that boiled egg white and sorghum porridge contain protein, because both turned violet or purple, and that the sugar solution does not, because it stayed blue. The deep purple of the egg white means more protein than the pale lilac of the porridge, since the extracts were prepared in the same way.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the colours read correctly, egg white and porridge give a violet colour so contain protein, the sugar solution stayed blue so protein is not detected (1); the deeper colour means more protein in the egg white than in the porridge, given the same volume and method (1).
The test shows protein but not which protein, so a claim about the type of protein earns no mark.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a polar molecule.
items.canonical_answer: A polar molecule has an uneven distribution of charge, so that one region is slightly positive and another slightly negative.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the key words, uneven distribution of charge, with one slightly positive region and one slightly negative region. An answer that says the molecule is positively or negatively charged overall describes an ion.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: Explain how the polarity of water molecules leads to hydrogen bonds between them.
items.canonical_answer: Oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does, so each water molecule has a slightly negative oxygen and slightly positive hydrogens. The slightly positive hydrogen of one molecule is then attracted to the slightly negative oxygen of another molecule, and this attraction is a hydrogen bond.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the uneven charge, slightly negative oxygen and slightly positive hydrogen, because oxygen attracts the electrons more strongly (1); the attraction between the hydrogen of one molecule and the oxygen of another is the hydrogen bond (1).
A hydrogen bond between two molecules is the point; a hydrogen bond described inside a molecule earns no mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: A learner says that the hydrogen bonds in water are the bonds between the hydrogen and oxygen atoms inside each water molecule. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is a confusion of the bonds inside a molecule with the bonds between molecules. The bonds inside a water molecule are covalent O–H bonds. In fact a hydrogen bond forms between the slightly positive hydrogen of one molecule and the slightly negative oxygen of a different molecule. The test is to ask whether the bond is within one molecule or between two: a hydrogen bond is between two.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, covalent bonds inside the molecule called hydrogen bonds (1); the correct idea, a hydrogen bond is between the hydrogen of one molecule and the oxygen of another (1).
The card discriminates within one molecule from between two molecules, and it is not a repeat of the definition of polarity.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: A learner writes that cohesion is the attraction between water and the walls of a cell, and adhesion is the attraction between water molecules. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is that the two terms are reversed. In fact cohesion is the attraction between water molecules, caused by hydrogen bonds, and adhesion is the attraction between water and other surfaces, such as cell walls. The test is to ask whether the attraction is between water molecules or between water and another surface: water to water is cohesion, and water to another surface is adhesion.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, the two terms reversed (1); the correct pair, cohesion is water to water by hydrogen bonds, adhesion is water to another surface such as a cell wall (1).
The card discriminates the two terms by what is attracted to what; the hydrogen bonds belong to cohesion.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.4.2 from its claim ledger. Our own scenarios and wording; unverified.

items.prompt: Describe the feature of water molecules that makes water a solvent for ions and other polar substances in cells.
items.canonical_answer: Water molecules are polar, with a slightly negative oxygen and slightly positive hydrogens. They are attracted to the charges on ions and polar molecules and surround each one, which separates it from the others so that it dissolves.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the feature, water molecules are polar (slightly negative oxygen, slightly positive hydrogens), attracted to ions and polar substances (1); the water molecules surround and separate each particle, so it dissolves (1).
A statement that water dissolves everything is not accepted: non-polar substances such as lipids dissolve poorly.

items.prompt: Explain how the large latent heat of vaporisation of water helps a goat to cool down when it is overheated.
items.canonical_answer: The goat sweats, and the sweat evaporates from the skin. Evaporation needs a large amount of energy to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules, which is the latent heat of vaporisation. The energy is taken from the skin, so the skin cools.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the sweat evaporates, which needs a large amount of energy to break hydrogen bonds (1); the energy is taken from the skin, so the skin cools (1).
The cooling depends on evaporation. A statement that the sweat is cold, or that water has a high specific heat capacity, does not answer the question.

items.prompt:
Twelve questions. Choose one option for each.

1. Which option lists the four things bonded to the central carbon atom of an amino acid?
A  an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydroxyl group and an R group
B  an amino group, a carboxyl group, a phosphate group and an R group
C  an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R group
D  two amino groups, a carboxyl group and a hydrogen atom

2. Two amino acids join in a condensation reaction to form a dipeptide. Which statement is correct?
A  A molecule of water is released and a peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the other.
B  A molecule of water is added and a peptide bond forms between the two R groups.
C  A molecule of water is released and a peptide bond forms between the two R groups.
D  A molecule of water is added and a peptide bond forms between the carboxyl groups of both amino acids.

3. A protease breaks a peptide bond in a polypeptide. Which reaction occurs?
A  condensation, which releases a molecule of water
B  hydrolysis, which uses a molecule of water
C  hydrolysis, which releases a molecule of water
D  condensation, which uses a molecule of water

4. Which bond in a protein is covalent and forms between the sulfur atoms of the R groups of two cysteines?
A  hydrogen bond
B  ionic bond
C  disulfide bond
D  hydrophobic interaction

5. In a folded protein that works in water, where are most of the non-polar R groups found?
A  on the outer surface, in contact with water
B  in the interior, away from water
C  in the peptide bonds
D  in the carboxyl group at the end of the chain

6. A polypeptide has a lysine R group with a positive charge (–NH3+) and an aspartic acid R group with a negative charge (–COO–). The folding brings them close together. Which interaction forms between them?
A  a disulfide bond
B  a hydrophobic interaction
C  a peptide bond
D  an ionic bond

7. In a water molecule, which atom carries a slight negative charge, and why?
A  hydrogen, because it attracts the shared electrons
B  oxygen, because it attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does
C  oxygen, because it has transferred electrons to hydrogen
D  hydrogen, because it has gained electrons from oxygen

8. Which statement describes a hydrogen bond in water?
A  It is an attraction between the slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule and the slightly negative oxygen of another.
B  It is a covalent bond between a hydrogen atom and the oxygen atom inside one water molecule.
C  It is an attraction between the slightly positive hydrogens of two neighbouring water molecules.
D  It is a bond formed when two oxygen atoms share electrons.

9. A diagram shows one water molecule at the centre. Each of its two hydrogen atoms is close to the oxygen of a different neighbour, and its oxygen is close to a hydrogen atom of each of two further neighbours. How many hydrogen bonds does the central molecule form in the diagram?
A  2
B  3
C  4
D  6

10. Water clings to the clean glass wall of a beaker and the water level curves up at the edge. Which term describes the attraction between the water and the glass?
A  cohesion
B  adhesion
C  hydrolysis
D  solvent action

11. On a sunny day the water in a pond warms more slowly than the dry sand beside it. Which statement explains this?
A  Water has a low specific heat capacity, so the energy is spread through the whole pond.
B  Water is a good solvent, so the energy is used to dissolve substances.
C  Water has a large latent heat of vaporisation, so the pond cools as it warms.
D  Water has a high specific heat capacity, so a large amount of energy is needed to raise its temperature.

12. Sweat evaporating from the skin of a goat in hot sun cools the goat. Which statement explains this?
A  Evaporation takes in a large amount of energy from the skin to break hydrogen bonds, because water has a large latent heat of vaporisation.
B  Sweat has a high specific heat capacity, so it stays cooler than the skin.
C  Sweat dissolves heat from the skin, because water is a good solvent.
D  Evaporation releases hydrogen bonds, which gives out heat to the air.
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 C, 2 A, 3 B, 4 C, 5 B, 6 D, 7 B, 8 A, 9 C, 10 B, 11 D, 12 A.
1. The central carbon bears an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R group (C). A names a hydroxyl group, which is already part of the carboxyl group; B brings in a phosphate group, which belongs to other molecules such as ATP; D has two amino groups and omits the R group.
2. Condensation releases water and joins the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of the other (A). B and D say water is added, which is hydrolysis, and put the bond in the wrong place; C has water released but joins the R groups, which are not the groups that form the peptide bond.
3. Breaking a peptide bond is hydrolysis, which uses a molecule of water (B). A and D name condensation, the reaction that forms the bond; C names the right reaction but reverses the water, since hydrolysis uses water instead of releasing it.
4. The covalent bond between two sulfur atoms is the disulfide bond (C). A is the weak attraction involving hydrogen, the usual confusion with disulfide; B is between oppositely charged R groups; D is a clustering of non-polar R groups, not a bond between atoms.
5. Non-polar R groups cluster in the interior, away from the water (B). A reverses the arrangement, which describes the polar R groups; C and D place R groups in the backbone, but R groups are side chains, not parts of the peptide bond or the terminal groups.
6. Opposite charges on two R groups form an ionic bond (D). A needs sulfur atoms from two cysteines; B is for non-polar R groups, which carry no charge; C joins the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, not two R groups.
7. Oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly, so it is slightly negative (B). A has the right reason on the wrong atom; C and D describe an ionic transfer of electrons, but the O–H bonds are covalent, so electrons are shared unequally and not transferred.
8. A hydrogen bond is between the hydrogen of one molecule and the oxygen of another (A). B describes the covalent O–H bond inside a molecule, the most common confusion; C joins two atoms of the same charge, which repel; D describes an O–O bond that water does not have.
9. Two bonds through the hydrogens and two through the oxygen make 2 + 2 = 4 hydrogen bonds (C). A counts only the bonds through the hydrogen atoms; B is a miscount of the neighbours; D adds the two covalent O–H bonds inside the molecule, 4 + 2 = 6, which are not hydrogen bonds.
10. Attraction between water and another surface, here glass, is adhesion (B). A is the attraction between water molecules, the reversed term; C is a reaction that uses water; D describes dissolving, not clinging.
11. A high specific heat capacity means a large energy input is needed for each degree of warming, partly to loosen hydrogen bonds (D). A states the property wrongly as low; B confuses solvent action with heat capacity; C names latent heat, which concerns evaporation, not the rate of warming.
12. Evaporation absorbs energy from the skin to break hydrogen bonds, which cools it (A). B wrongly uses specific heat capacity, a property about warming, not evaporating; C misapplies solvent action, since heat is not a solute; D reverses the energy flow, because breaking bonds takes in energy and does not release it.
marking_guidance: The key: one mark per correct option, twelve marks in all; about half the questions test recall and half test application to a described diagram, structure, pond or animal.

Each distractor is a named error: dipeptide bond and peptide bond confused, condensation and hydrolysis reversed, disulfide and hydrogen bonds confused, bonds inside a molecule called hydrogen bonds (the misconception register first), cohesion and adhesion reversed, and specific heat capacity confused with latent heat.

items.prompt:
A farmer in the Kavango region takes a blood sample from a goat and breaks open the red blood cells to release their contents. The extract is red. She adds sodium hydroxide solution to a sample of the extract, then a few drops of dilute copper(II) sulfate solution. The mixture turns violet. The main protein in the extract is haemoglobin.

(a) State the colour of the mixture if the extract had contained no protein. [1]
(b) Explain why the extract gave a violet colour. [2]
(c) State the importance of the iron in a haemoglobin molecule. [1]
(d) Describe how the structure of the haemoglobin molecule makes it soluble in the cytoplasm of a red blood cell. [2]
(e) The goat is later fed a diet with very little iron. Suggest why the goat becomes tired more easily. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Blue.
(b) The extract contains protein, and protein has peptide bonds. In the alkaline mixture, copper(II) ions bind to the nitrogen atoms of the peptide bonds and form a violet complex.
(c) Each haem group contains an Fe2+ ion, which binds one oxygen molecule, so haemoglobin can carry oxygen.
(d) Haemoglobin is a globular protein, a compact molecule folded so that the non-polar R groups are in the interior and the polar R groups are on the outside. The polar outer surface is attracted to water, so the molecule dissolves.
(e) Iron is needed to make haem, so less haemoglobin is made. The blood then carries less oxygen to the muscles, so less aerobic respiration can take place and less energy is released, and the goat tires easily.
marking_guidance: Marks and points: (a) 1 mark for blue; (b) 2 marks from three points: protein contains peptide bonds, copper(II) ions bind to the peptide bonds in alkaline conditions, a violet complex forms; (c) 1 mark for iron (Fe2+) binding oxygen.

(d) 2 marks from three points: globular, compact; non-polar R groups inside; polar R groups outside attracted to water, which is the reason it dissolves. (e) 2 marks from three points: less iron means less haem or haemoglobin, so less oxygen carried, because less oxygen reaches the muscles for aerobic respiration. Parts (a) and (c) credit AO A (2 marks); parts (b), (d) and (e) credit AO B (6 marks). Each reason must use the information given, and each term, such as polar, must be used correctly.
